questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the tangent to the curve $y=(2 x-1) e^{2(1-x)}$ at the point of its maximum, is
questions.solution:
We have,
$y=(2 x-1) e^{2(1-x)}$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} & =2 e^{2(1-x)}-2(2 x-1) e^{2(1-x)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d x} & =2 e^{2(1-x)}(2-2 x)=4 e^{2(1-x)}(1-x)\end{aligned}$
At points of maximum, we must have
$\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \Rightarrow x=1$
Now,
$\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-8 e^{2(1-x)}(1-x)-4 e^{2(1-x)}\Rightarrow \quad\left[\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right]_{x=1}=-4 \lt 0$
So, $y$ is maximum at $x=1$. Clearly, $y=1$ for $x=1$.
Thus, the point of maximum is $(1,1)$.
The equation is the tangent at $(1,1)$ is
$y-1=0(x-1)\Rightarrow \quad y=1$

At the point where the given curve crosses $X$-axis, we have
$y=0\Rightarrow \quad a x^2=1$
[putting $y=0$ in $a x^2+2 h y x+b y^2=1$ ]
$\Rightarrow \quad x= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$
Thus, the given curve cuts $X$-axis at $P\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, 0\right)$ and
$Q\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, 0\right)$.
Now, $a x^2+2 h x y+b y^2=1$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get
$2 a x+2 h\left(x \frac{d y}{d x}+y\right)+2 b y \frac{d y}{d x}=0\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{a x+h y}{h x+b y} \\ \Rightarrow & {\left[\frac{d y}{d x}\right]_P=-\frac{a}{h} \text { and }\left[\frac{d y}{d x}\right]_Q=-\frac{a}{h}} \\ \Rightarrow & {\left[\frac{d y}{d x}\right]_p=\left[\frac{d y}{d x}\right]_Q}\end{array}$
Hence, the tangents are parallel.

questions.solution:
Let $y=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}{x}\right)$
Putting $x=\tan \theta$, we get
$\begin{aligned} y & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\sec \theta-1}{\tan \theta}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left(\tan \frac{\theta}{2}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \tan ^{-1} x\end{aligned}$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t. x , we get
$\begin{array}{r}\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{2\left(1+x^2\right)} \\ \text { and } z=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 x \sqrt{1-x^2}}{1-2 x^2}\right)\end{array}
Putting $x=\sin \theta$, we get

On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\frac{d z}{d x}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$
Thus, $\frac{d y}{d z}=\frac{d y / d x}{d z / d x}=\frac{1}{4\left(1+x^2\right)} \sqrt{1-x^2}\therefore \quad\left[\frac{d y}{d z}\right]_{x=0}=\frac{1}{4}

Hence, required probability $=\frac{6 \times 3!}{100^3}$

questions.q: If an isosceles triangle of vertical angle $2 \theta$ is inscribed in a circle of radius $a$. Then, area of the triangle is maximum, when $\theta$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have, $A D=a+a \cos 2 \theta \text { and } B C=2 B D=2 a \sin 2 \theta\therefore$ Area of $\triangle A B C$ is given by $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} B C \times A D=\frac{2}{2} a^2(\sin 2 \theta+\sin 2 \theta \cos 2 \theta)\Rightarrow \quad \Delta=a^2 \sin 2 \theta+\frac{1}{2} a^2 \sin 4 \theta$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $\theta$, we get $\frac{d \Delta}{d \theta}=2 a^2 \cos 2 \theta+2 a^2 \cos 4 \theta$ For maximum or minimum, put $\frac{d \Delta}{d \theta}=0$. $\begin{array}{rlrl}\Rightarrow & \cos 2 \theta & =-\cos 4 \theta \\ \Rightarrow & & 2 \theta & =\pi-4 \theta \\ \Rightarrow & & \theta & =\frac{\pi}{6}\end{array}$ Now, $\frac{d^2 \Delta}{d \theta^2}=-2 a^2 \sin 2 \theta \times 2-2 a^2 \sin 4 \theta \times 4=-4 a^2 \sin 2 \theta-8 a^2 \sin 4 \theta$ At $\quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{d^2 \Delta}{d \theta^2}=-4 a^2 \sin \frac{\pi}{3}-8 a^2 \sin \frac{2 \pi}{3}\begin{aligned} & =-4 a^2 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-8 a^2 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & =-6 a^2 \sqrt{3} \lt 0\end{aligned}$ Hence, $\Delta$ is maximum for $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

questions.q: In a $\triangle A B C$, if $a^2+b^2+c^2=a c+\sqrt{3} a b$, then the triangle is
questions.solution:
We have, $a^2+b^2+c^2=a c+\sqrt{3} a b\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{a^2}{4}+c^2-a c+\frac{3 a^2}{4}+b^2-\sqrt{3} a b=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{a}{2}-c\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} a}{2}-b\right)^2=0\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{a}{2}-c=0 \text { and } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a-b=0 \\ \Rightarrow & a=2 c \text { and } \sqrt{3} a=2 b \\ \Rightarrow & a=\frac{2 b}{\sqrt{3}}=2 c=\lambda \\ \Rightarrow & a=\lambda, b=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \lambda \text { and } c=\frac{\lambda}{2}\end{array}$
Now, $b^2+c^2=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} \lambda}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)^2=\frac{3 \lambda^2}{a}+\frac{\lambda^2}{4}=\lambda^2\therefore \quad b^2+c^2=a^2$
Hence, the triangle is right angled but not isosceles.

questions.q: Let a,b and c be non-zero vectors such that no two are collinear and $(a \times b) \times c=\frac{1}{3}|b||c| a$. If $\theta$ is the acute angle between the vectors $b$ and $c$, then $\sin \theta$ equals
questions.solution:
We have,
$(a \times b) \times c=\frac{1}{3}|b||c| a\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & (a \cdot c) b-(b \cdot c) a=\frac{1}{3}|b||c| a \\ \Rightarrow \quad & (a \cdot c) b-\left\{(b \cdot c)+\frac{1}{3}|b||c|\right\} a=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & a \cdot c=0 \text { and } b \cdot c+\frac{1}{3}|b||c|=0 \\ & {[\because a, b \text { are non-collinear }] }\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad|\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}| \cos \theta+\frac{1}{3}|\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \cos \theta=-\frac{1}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta=\sqrt{1-\cos ^2 \theta}=\sqrt{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^2}\end{aligned}=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{9}}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{9}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The alternating voltage and current in an electric circuit are respectively given by $E=100 \sin 100 \pi t, I=5 \sin 100 \pi t$
The reactance of the circuit will be
questions.solution:
The general equations of alternating voltage and current in an AC circuit are as follows
$E=E_0 \sin \omega t$  ...(i)
$I=I_0 \sin \omega t$  ...(ii)
Given that,
$E=100 \sin 100 \pi t$  ...(iii)
$I=5 \sin 100 \pi t$  ...(iv)
Comparing Eqs. (ii) and and (iv), we get, Peak value of current, $I_0=5 \mathrm{~A}$ Comparing Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get Peak value of voltage, $E_0=100 \mathrm{~V}$ Now, r.m.s. value of voltage is given by
$E_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~V}$
Similarly, r.m.s. value of current is given by
$I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~A}$
Hence, reactance of the circuit is given by
$Z=\frac{E_{\mathrm{rms}}}{I_{\mathrm{rms}}}=\frac{\frac{100}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}}=20 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If levels 1 and 2 are separated by an energy $E_2-E_1$, such that the corresponding transition frequency falls in the middle of the visible range, calculate the ratio of the populations of two levels in the thermal equilibrium at room temperature.
questions.solution:
At thermal equilibrium, the ratio $\frac{N_2}{N_1}$ is given as $\frac{N_2}{N_1}=\exp \left(-\frac{E_2-E_1}{k T}\right)$
The middle of the visible range is taken at $\begin{array}{ll} \lambda=550 \mathrm{~nm} \\ \Rightarrow & E_2-E_1=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=3.16 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{N_2}{N_1}=\exp \left(\frac{-3.16 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}}{\left(1.38 \times 10^{-23} 1 / \mathrm{k}\right) \cdot(300 \mathrm{k})}\right) \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{N_2}{N_1}=1.1577 \times 10^{-38} \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is -13.6 eV . The energy of the level corresponding to the quantum number $n=5$ is
questions.solution:
The energy of the hydrogen atom in nth state is givne by
$E_n=\frac{-13.6}{\left(n^2\right)} \mathrm{eV}$
Here, $\quad n=5\therefore \quad E=\frac{-13.6}{(5)^2} \mathrm{eV}=-0.54 \mathrm{eV}$

questions.solution:
Charge acquired by the plates of the capacitor $q_0=C V=(10 \mu \mathrm{~F}) \times(50 \mathrm{~V})=500 \mu \mathrm{C}$
Now, let the charge distribution is as follows. Total charge on positive plate has now become $700 \mu \mathrm{C}$ while that in negative plate is still $-500 \mu \mathrm{C}$,
Here, charges are in $\mu \mathrm{C}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A neutron moving with a speed $v$ makes a head on collision with a hydrogen atom in ground state kept at rest. The minimum kinetic energy of neutron for which inelastic collision will take place is
questions.solution:
Let $v=$ speed of neutron before collision
$v_1=$ speed of neutron after collision
$v_2=$ speed of hydrogen atom after collision and
$\Delta E=$ energy of the excitation
From the conservation of linear momentum,
$m v=m v_1+m v_2$  ...(i)
From the conservation of energy,
$\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2+\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2+\Delta E$  ...(ii)
from Eq. (i),
$v^2=v_1^2+v_2^2+2 v_1 v_2$
From Eq. (ii),
$\begin{array}{rlrl} & & v^2 & =v_1^2+v_2^2+\frac{2 \Delta E}{m} \\ & \therefore & 2 v_1 v_2 & =\frac{2 \Delta E}{m} \\ & \therefore & \left(v_1-v_2\right)^2 & =\left(v_1+v_2\right)^2-4 v_1 v_2 \\ & & =v^2-\frac{4 \Delta E}{m}\end{array}
As, $v_1-v_2$ must be real
$\Rightarrow \quad v^2-\frac{4 \Delta E}{m} \geq 0$
or
$\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \geq 2 \Delta E$
The maximum energy that can be absorbed by hydrogen atom in ground state to go into excited state is 10.2 eV . Therefore, the minimum kinetic energy required is
$\frac{1}{2} m v_{\min }^2=2 \times 10.2 \mathrm{eV}=20.4 \mathrm{eV}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A ball is projected from the point $O$ with velocity $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with horizontal as shown in the figure. At highest point of its trajectory, it strikes a smooth plane of inclination $30^{\circ}$ at point $A$. The collision is perfectly inelastic. The maximum height from the ground attained by the ball is
questions.solution:
Speed of ball before collision is $v=u \cos 60^{\circ}=20 \times \frac{1}{2}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Since, collision is perfectly inelastic ( $e=0$ ), so the ball will not bounce. It will move along the plane with velocity
$v^{\prime}=v \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{10 \sqrt{3}}{2}=5 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\therefore$ Maximum height attained by the ball $\begin{aligned} H & =\frac{u^2 \sin ^2 60^{\circ}}{2 g}+\frac{v^{\prime 2}}{2 g} \\ H & =\frac{(20)^2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2}{20}+\frac{(5 \sqrt{3})^2}{20} \\ & =\frac{300}{20}+\frac{75}{20}=18.75 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: We have a galvanometer of resistance $25 \Omega$. It is shunted by $2.5 \Omega$ wire. The part of the total current that flows through the galvanometer is given as
questions.solution:
When a galvanometer is connected to the shunt resistance, then we have potential drop across the galvanometer = potential drop across the shunt
i.e.
$i G=\left(i-i_0\right) S$  ...(i)
Here, $i=$ current through the galvanometer
$G=$ resistance of the galvanometer
$i_0=$ current through the shunt resistance
$S=$ shunt resistance
From Eq. (i), we have the part of the total current that flows through the galvanometer is
$\frac{i}{i_0}=\frac{S}{G+S}$
Substituting, $S=2.5 \Omega, G=25 \Omega$, we get
$\frac{i}{i_0}=\frac{1}{11}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil having $n$ turns and resistance $R \Omega$ is connected with a galvanometer of resistance $4 R \Omega$. This combination is moved in time $t$ second from a magnetic field $w_1$ weber to $w_2$ weber. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
Current is given by $I=\frac{E}{R^{\prime}}$
Substituting, $E=-\frac{n d \phi}{d t}$, we get $I=-\frac{n}{R^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{d \phi}{d t}$ ...(i) Given that $w_1$ and $w_2$ are the values of the flux associated with one turn of the coil.
Therefore, Eq. (i) becomes, $I=-\frac{n}{R^{\prime}}\left[\frac{w_2-w_1}{t_2-t_1}\right]$ ...(ii) Total resistance of the combination is $R^{\prime}=R+4 R=5 R$, substituting the values of $R^{\prime}$ and $\left(t_2-t_1\right)=t$ in Eq. (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad & I=-\frac{n}{5 R}\left(\frac{w_2-w_1}{t}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad & I=\frac{-n\left(w_2-w_1\right)}{5 R t}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The length of a potentiometer wire is 1 . A cell of emf $E$ is balanced at length $1 / 3$ from the positive end of the wire. If the length of the wire is increased by $1 / 2$. Then, at what distance will the same cell give a balance point?
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the desired length.
Potential gradient in the first case $=\frac{E_0}{l}E=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \cdot\left(\frac{E_0}{1}\right)=\frac{E_0}{3}$ ...(i) Potential gradient in the second case. $=\frac{E_0}{31 / 2}=\frac{2 E_0}{31}\therefore \quad E=(x) \frac{2 E_0}{31}$ ...(ii) From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{E_0}{3}=\left(\frac{2 E_0}{31}\right) x\Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Under what conditions current passing through the resistance $R$ can be increased by short circuiting the battery of emf $E_2$ ? The internal resistances of the two batteries are $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively.
questions.solution:
The current through the circuit before the battery of emf $E_2$ is short circuited, is
$i_1=\frac{E_1+E_2}{r_1+r_2+R}$  ...(i)
After short circuiting the battery of emf $E_2$, current through the resistance $R$ would be
$i_2=\frac{E_1}{R+I_1}$  ...(ii)
Since, from Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$i_2 \gt i_1\therefore \quad \frac{E_1}{R+r_1} \gt \frac{E_1+E_2}{R+r_1+r_2}$
This gives $\quad E_1 r_2 \gt E_2\left(R+r_1\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Out of a photon and an electron, the equation $E=P C$, is valid for
questions.solution:
Energy is given by
$E=\frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}\Rightarrow \quad E^2=\frac{m_0^2 c^6}{c^2-v^2}$
Momentum $P$ is given by
$P=\frac{m_0 v}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)}}P^2 c^2=\frac{m_0^2 c^4 v^2}{c^2-v^2}\begin{aligned} & \therefore & E^2-P^2 c^2 & =m_0^2 c^4 \\ \Rightarrow & & E^2 & =P^2 c^2+m_0^2 c^4\end{aligned}$
For photon, rest mass
$m_0=0, \quad$ so $E=P c$
For electron, $\quad m_0 \neq 0$, so $E \neq P c$

questions.q: In wave mechanics, the angular momentum of an electron is given by
questions.solution:
In wave mechanics, the magnitude of angular momentum of an electron is
$L=\sqrt{l(l+1) \frac{h}{2 \pi}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find the frequency of light which ejects electron from a metal surface fully stopped by a retarding potential of 3 V . The photoelectric effect begins in this metal at a frequency of $6 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}$.
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation,
$E=h v-w$
If $V_s$ is retarding or stopping potential and $v_0$ is the threshold frequency, then the above equation becomes
$\begin{aligned} e V_s & =h v-h v_0 \\ h v & =e V_s+h v_0 \\ v & =\frac{e V_s}{h}+v_0\end{aligned}$
Hence, $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}V_s=3 \mathrm{~V}, v_0=6 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~Hz}$
Therefore, required frequency,
$\begin{aligned} v & =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 3}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}+6 \times 10^{14} \\ & =\frac{4.8}{6.63} \times 10^{15}+6 \times 10^{14} \\ & =0.723 \times 10^{15}+6 \times 10^{14} \\ & =7.23 \times 10^{14}+6 \times 10^{14} \\ & =13.23 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz} \\ & =1.323 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~Hz}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The time constant of $L-R$ circuit is
questions.solution:
The instantaneous current in $L-R$ circuit during growth is given by $I=I_0\left(1-e^{-\frac{R_t}{L}}\right)$
Since, all the exponential terms are dimensionless, therefore, it follows that factor $\frac{R}{L} t$ should be dimensionless i.e. $\frac{R}{L} t=\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0\right]\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{R}{L}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0\right]}{[\mathrm{T}]}=\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right] \\ \Rightarrow & {\left[\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}}\right]=[\mathrm{T}]}\end{array}$ Hence, the time constant of $L-R$ circuit is $\left[\frac{L}{R}\right]$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find the inductance of a unit length of two parallel wires, each of radius $a$, whose centres are at distance $d$ apart and carry equal currents in opposite directions. Neglect the flux within the wire.
questions.solution:
Since, the wires are infinite, so the system of these two wires can be considered as closed rectangle of infinite length and breadth equal to $d$. Flux through strip $\phi=\int_a^{d-a} \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}(l d r)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi} \ln \left(\frac{d-a}{a}\right)$
The other wire produces the same result, so the total flux through the rectangle $A B C D$ is $\phi_{\text {total }}=\frac{\mu_0 I I}{\pi} \ln \left(\frac{d-a}{a}\right)$ The total inductance of length 1 $L=\frac{I_{\text {total }}}{I}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi} \ln \left(\frac{d-a}{a}\right)$ Inductance per unit length $=\frac{L}{l}=\frac{\mu_0}{\pi} \ln \left(\frac{d-a}{a}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils have mutual inductance 0.005 H . The current changes in the first coil according to equation $I=I_0 \sin \omega t$, where $I_0=10 \mathrm{~A}$ and $\omega=100 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The maximum value of emf in the second coil is
questions.solution:
The instantaneous current in the AC circuit is given by $I=I_0 \sin \omega t\begin{aligned} & \frac{d I}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(I_0 \sin \omega t\right) \\ & \frac{d I}{d t}=\left(I_0 \cos \omega t\right) \omega \end{aligned}$ Substituting $\quad I_0=10 \mathrm{~A}, \omega=100 \pi\begin{aligned} \cos (100 \pi) & =1, \text { we get } \\ \frac{d I}{d t} & =1000 \pi \end{aligned}$
Hence, induced emf is given by $E=M \frac{d I}{d t}$
On putting $M=0.005 \mathrm{H}, \frac{d I}{d t}=1000 \pi$, we get $E=(5 \pi) \mathrm{V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron beam accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 5000 V in vaccum is allowed to impinge on a surface normally. The incident current is $50 \mu \mathrm{~A}$ and if the electron comes to rest on striking the surface, the force on it is
questions.solution:
Energy $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=5000 \mathrm{eV}\begin{aligned} & =5000 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\ m v_2 & =\sqrt{2 \times 5000 \times\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)} \mathrm{m} \\ & =4 \times 10^{-8} \sqrt{m}\end{aligned}$
Number of electrons striking per second is
$\begin{aligned} & n=\frac{q}{e}=\frac{I t}{e}=\frac{50 \times 10^{-6} \times 1}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad n & =31.25 \times 10^{13}\end{aligned}$
Force = Change of momentum per second
$\begin{aligned} & =n(m v)=31.25 \times 10^{13} \times 4 \times 10^{-8} \sqrt{m} \\ & =125 \times 10^5 \sqrt{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}=1.1924 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~N}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point charges $2 q$ and $8 q$ are placed at a distance $r$ apart. Where should a third charge $-q$ be placed between them, so that the electrical potential energy of the system is minimum?
options: At a distance of $r / 3$ from $2 q$
At a distance of $2 r / 3$ from $2 q$
At a distance of $r / 16$ from $2 q$
questions.solution:
Let the third charge $-q$ is placed at a distance of $x$ from the charge $2 q$. Then, the potential energy of the system is
$U=k\left[\frac{2 q(8 q)}{r}-\frac{(2 q)(q)}{x}-\frac{(8 q)(q)}{r-x}\right]$
Here, $\quad k=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}U$ is minimum, where $\frac{2}{x}+\frac{8}{r-x}$ is maximum
Let
$\frac{2}{x}+\frac{8}{r-x}=y$
For $y$ to be maximum, $\frac{d y}{d x}=0-\frac{2}{x^2}+\frac{8}{(r-x)^2}=0\Rightarrow \quad \frac{x}{r-x}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x=\frac{r}{3}$
But at $x=\frac{r}{3}, \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=$ positive i.e. at $x=\frac{r}{3}, y$ is minimum or $U$ is maximum. So, there cannot be any point between them where the potential energy is minimum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a given density of a planet, the orbital speed of satellite near the surface of the planet of radius $R$ is proportional to
questions.solution:
Applying Newton's second law to a circular orbit, we have
$\frac{m v^2}{r}=\frac{4 \pi^2 r m}{T^2}=\frac{G M m}{r^2}$
where, $m$ is the mass of satellite, and $v$ is the orbital speed
$T$ is the time period
$\therefore \quad T=\frac{2 \pi r^{3 / 2}}{\sqrt{G M}}$
For $r \approx R$
and $M=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \rho(\rho=$ density of planet $)T=\sqrt{\frac{3 \pi}{\rho G}}$
i.e. $T$ is independent of $R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the energy required to raise a satellite upto a height $h$ above the earth to the kinetic energy of the satellite into the orbit is
questions.solution:
Energy required to raise a satellite upto a height $h$,
$E_1=\Delta U=\frac{m g h}{1+\frac{h}{R}}$  ...(i)
$E_2=$ energy required to put in orbit
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{G M}{r}\right) \text { as } v_0=\text { orbital speed } \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{G M}{R+h}\right)=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{G M}{R^2}\right) \frac{R}{1+\frac{h}{R}}\end{aligned}$  ...(ii)
$\Rightarrow \quad E_2=\frac{m g R}{2\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{2 h}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The specific heat at constant volume for the monoatomic argon is $0.075 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}-\mathrm{K}$, whereas its gram molecular specific heat is $C_V=2.98 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{mol} \mathrm{K}$. The mass of the carbon atom is
questions.solution:
Molar specific heat
$=$ Molecular weight \times  gram specific heat.
$C_V=M \times C_V\begin{aligned} 2.98 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{mol}-\mathrm{K} & =M \times 0.075 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}-\mathrm{K} \\ & =\frac{M \times 0.075 \times 10^3}{10^3} \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{K}\end{aligned}\therefore$ Molecular weight of argon,
$M=\frac{2.98}{0.075}=39.7 \mathrm{~g}$
i.e. mass of $6.023 \times 10^{23}$ atom $=39.7 \mathrm{~g}$
Therefore, mass of
$\begin{aligned}
\text { single atom } & =\frac{39.7}{6.023 \times 10^{23}} \\
& =6.60 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two moles of helium are mixed with $n$ moles of hydrogen. The root mean square (rms) speed of gas molecules in the mixture is $\sqrt{2}$ times the speed of sound in the mixture. Then, the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
$\because v_{\text {mis }}=\sqrt{\frac{3 R T}{M}}$ and $v_{\text {sound }}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}}$,
$v_{\mathrm{rms}}=2 v_{\text {sound }}$
i.e. $\quad \gamma=\frac{3}{2}=$ ratio of $\frac{C_p}{C_V}$ for the mixture
$C_V=\frac{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}}{n_1+n_2}$
and
$C_p=\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1+n_2}\therefore \quad \gamma=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}}\therefore \quad \frac{3}{2}=\frac{2\left(\frac{5}{2} R\right)+n\left(\frac{7}{2} R\right)}{2\left(\frac{3}{2} R\right)+n\left(\frac{5}{2} R\right)}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{3}{2}=\frac{10+7 n}{6+5 n} \\ \Rightarrow & n=2\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A large slab of mass 5 kg lies on a smooth horizontal surface, with a block of mass 4 kg lying on the top of it, the coefficient of friction between the block and the slab is Q.25. If the block is pulled horizontally by a force of $F=6 \mathrm{~N}$, the work done by the force of friction on the slab between the instants $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ and $t=3 \mathrm{~s}$ is
questions.solution:
Maximum frictional force between the slab and the block $f_{\max }=\mu N=\mu m g=\frac{1}{4} \times 4 \times 10=10 \mathrm{~N}$
Evidently, $f \propto f_{\max }$ So, the two bodies will move together as a single unit. If a be their combined acceleration, then $a=\frac{F}{m+M}=\frac{6}{4+5}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ Therefore, frictional force acting can be obtained as $f=M a=\frac{2}{3} \times 5=\frac{10}{3} N$ Using $\quad S=\frac{1}{2} a t^2S(2)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{3}(2)^2=\frac{4}{3}$ and $\quad S(3)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{3} \times(3)^2=3$ Therefore, work done by friction $=F[S(3)-S(2)]=\frac{10}{3}\left[3-\frac{4}{3}\right]=\frac{50}{9}=5.55 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is lying on the edge having inclination angle $\alpha=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)$. Wedge is moving with a constant acceleration, $a=2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$. The minimum value of coefficient of friction $\mu$, so that $m$ remains stationary with respect to wedge is

questions.q: A circular coil of 100 turns has an effective radius of 0.05 m and carries a current of 0.1 A . How much work is required to turn it in an external magnetic field of $1.5 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$ through $180^{\circ}$ about its axis perpendicular to the magnetic field? The plane of the coil is initially perpendicular to the magnetic field.
questions.solution:
The potential energy of circular loop in the magnetic field $=-M B \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between normal to plane of coil and magnetic field $B$. Initial potential energy, $U_i=-N i A B \cos 0^{\circ}=-N i A B$
When coil is turned through $180^{\circ}$, therefore final potential energy, $U_f=-N i A B \cos 180^{\circ}=N i A B\therefore$ Required work, $W=$ gain in potential energy $=U_f-U_i=N i A B-(-N i A B)=2NiAB$
Here, $N=100, \quad i=0.1 \mathrm{~A}, \quad B=1.5 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$ and radius $r=0.05 \mathrm{~m}\therefore \quad A=\pi r^2=3.14 \times(0.05)^2=7.85 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2\therefore$ Work, $\quad W=2 \times 100 \times 0.1 \times 7.85 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.5\Rightarrow \quad W=0.2355 \mathrm{~J}$

options: equal in radius, volume and density

Let $R$ be the radius of sphere, $V$ its volume and $\rho$ its density. Then,

and percentage change in radius
$\frac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100=100 \alpha \Delta \theta$  ...(i)
Now, $\quad \Delta V=\gamma v \Delta \theta=3 \alpha v \Delta \theta \quad\{\because \gamma=3 \alpha\}\therefore$ Percentage increase in volume

Again, $\quad \rho^{\prime}=\frac{\rho}{1+\gamma \Delta \theta}=\frac{\rho}{1+3 \alpha \Delta \theta}\therefore \quad \Delta \rho=\rho-\rho^{\prime}=\rho\left[1-\frac{1}{1+3 \alpha \Delta \theta}\right]=\frac{(3 \alpha \Delta \theta) \rho}{1+3 \alpha \Delta \theta}$
Percentage change in density
$=\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100=\frac{300 \alpha \Delta \theta}{1+3 \alpha \Delta \theta}$  ...(iii)
From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we see that the percentage change is maximum in volume.
